# The Intergenerational Health Effects of the Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals Program on Families With Mixed Immigration Status

**Authors:** Ghida El-Banna; Kimberly Higuera; Fernando S. Mendoza

**Affiliations:** Division of General Pediatrics, Stanford University School of Medicine, Center for Academic Medicine (G El-Banna and FS Mendoza), Palo Alto, Calif; Department of Sociology, Stanford University (K Higuera), Stanford, Calif; and Immigration Policy Lab, Stanford University, (FS Mendoza), Stanford, Calif

## Abstract

Children of undocumented mothers with Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals (DACA) have better mental health outcomes than children of DACA-ineligible mothers. This study explored the intergenerational health effects of DACA on undocumented parents and their children in families with mixed immigration status.

Forty-eight semistructured interviews were selected from a study on life transitions of 50 undocumented immigrants. Prevalent themes related to the intergenerational health effects of DACA on undocumented immigrants were identified through thematic analysis of the transcripts, and quotes were selected to illustrate themes in the participants’ own words.

Thirty-three of the 48 respondents were DACA recipients. Twenty-six respondents were parents with a total of 61 children, 73.8% of whom were US-born. Four themes were identified: 1) DACA recipients reported decreased familial stress because of protection from deportation and increased access to health care, 2) both DACA and DACA-ineligible parents prioritized regular pediatrician visits for their children, but DACA-ineligible parents suffered from poor health because of decreased access to health care, 3) adults with DACA mirror the health behaviors of their DACA-ineligible parents, and 4) the poor health access of DACA-ineligible family members appeared to stress DACA recipients and US-born children in these families.

DACA decreases children’s fear of parental deportation and loss. However, the suffering of DACA-ineligible parents and family members may stress their children and influence their health-seeking behavior in adulthood. Health care access for all members of immigrant families needs to be examined, since their well-being impacts the well-being of their children.

In 2018, there were 5.1 million children with at least one undocumented parent in the United States.1 This was more than 1 out of every 4 children in immigrant families, which made up 25% of all children in the United States. Among children with undocumented parents, 80% are US-born, 4% are documented immigrants, and 16% are undocumented (approximately 809,000).1 Parents’ and children’s immigration status is a significant social determinant of health that shapes children’s well-being by influencing family stability.1–5 Fear of parental deportation and anxiety about parental separation are chronic stressors for children of immigrants.

In 2012, the Obama administration established the Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals (DACA) program to provide deportation relief and social integration for undocumented immigrants, who arrived in the United States as children.6 A recent study demonstrated that US-born children of DACA-eligible mothers had a lower prevalence of mental health diagnoses compared to children of DACA-ineligible mothers.7 This suggests that DACA may have intergenerational effects on the well-being of children born to undocumented parents with DACA. The mechanism that links DACA to the well-being of children of immigrants deserves further investigation to better understand the pathways through which DACA can positively impact children.

Most studies on the benefits of DACA involve young adults, age 18 to 31, and show that DACA-eligible Latinos have had significant barriers to health care, including cost, access to health care, fear of deportation, and providers’ prejudice, with access to mental health resources being the greatest unmet need.8,9 Furthermore, qualitative research on mixed-status immigrant families has primarily explored how being undocumented—and thus vulnerable to deportation—negatively impacts the children of undocumented immigrants, but little research has explored how the DACA program affects children of DACA and DACA-ineligible adults.5,10

This study qualitatively investigated the utilization of health services by undocumented adults, with and without DACA, and for those who were parents, the reported health care usage of their children. We sought to characterize the different experiences of undocumented adults with respect to health care, and the effects of parental immigration status on their children’s health.

## Methods

### Design

This study is a health-focused secondary analysis of an institutional review board-approved qualitative study conducted by author K.H., exploring the life transitions of DACA and DACA-ineligible immigrants into their receiving communities. This “transition study” is hence-forth referred to as the “original study.”

### Sampling and Inclusion Criteria of the Original Study

Undocumented immigrants are a hard-to-reach population because of their vulnerability to immigration enforcement. The original study utilized a mix of snowball and targeted sampling to recruit this hard-to-reach population.11,12 Interviewees were recruited through prior studies’ contact lists, DACA workshops, immigrant serving organizations, community meetings, religious groups, and past interviewees’ referrals. DACA-ineligible interviewees were recruited by asking past interviewees to refer DACA-ineligible respondents as well as emphasizing the need for DACA-ineligible subjects during targeted recruitment.

Interviewers asked respondents whether they were currently enrolled in the DACA program or whether they were undocumented and hence had no type of permanent residential status or deportation protection. All respondents identified as “DACA” held a viable DACA permit at the time of the interview while those identified as “DACA-ineligible” were undocumented immigrants who did not meet the DACA program inclusion criteria.7 While not part of the inclusion criteria, interviewers also recorded subjects’ parental status and the immigration status of their children.

### Original Study Data Collection and Analysis

A semistructured interview protocol was designed for the original study by author K.H. and her doctoral advisor, Dr Tomás Jiménez. The interview protocol covered topics related to the impact of immigration status on participants’ daily life, their mental health, childhood experiences, and access to health resources. Included in the section on health-related experiences were additional questions for parents on parenting and their children’s health. Interviews were conducted in the interviewees’ preferred language, either Spanish or English. Respondents had the opportunity to elaborate on questions, so the interviews’ lengths varied from 1 to over 3 hours. Participants were interviewed in-person or over the telephone, which allowed for interviews with immigrants in 6 states. These 6 states represent both more established immigrant destinations (California, Arizona, and Illinois) and newer destinations (Kentucky, North Carolina, and Ohio).13,14 Interviews were collected between June 2017 and August 2018 by 4 trained interviewers. To ensure fidelity to respondents’ own words, interviews conducted in Spanish were transcribed into Spanish and then translated into English. Spanish and English transcripts were used for reference during analysis.

After each individual interview, the interviewer wrote a memo on key themes. Author K.H. thematically analyzed the transcripts in Dedoose (Los Angeles, Calif), a qualitative analysis software.15 Analysis started with a priori codes derived from the protocol themes while also allowing new codes to arise from the transcripts inductively.16,17 For the original study, thematic saturation was achieved with 50 subjects who were 33 DACA and 17 DACA-ineligible immigrants. Of the 50 subjects, 26 were parents and 24 were nonparents. The 24 nonparents were 22 adults with DACA and 2 who were DACA-ineligible adults.

### Health-Focused Analysis

The present study focused on the health experiences of undocumented immigrants with and without DACA, both as individuals and for those who had children, as parents. This analysis used 48 out of the 50 subjects in the original study, excluding 2 subjects who were DACA-ineligible and nonparents because of the small sample size of this category (N = 2). Among the 48 subjects included in the analysis, 33 subjects had DACA with 11 of these being parents, and 15 subjects were DACA-ineligible, all of whom were parents.

Codes were reviewed for this cohort with Dedoose and major themes related to health were identified.18 Both authors G.E. and K.H. independently reviewed the memos for each interview to identify the recurrent themes related to DACA’s effects on health seeking behavior. They then discussed the prevalent themes identified in the transcripts and memos and selected quotes from the original transcripts to illustrate themes in participants’ own words.19

## Results

Table 1 shows the characteristics of subjects by DACA status. Among the 48 subjects, 26 were parents (11 DACA and 15 DACA-ineligible) and 22 were nonparents (all DACA). Subjects with DACA were more likely to be female, English-speaking, younger, and more educated. Eighty-three percent of subjects were from Mexico and 75% resided in California.

DACA parents had fewer children than DACA-ineligible parents. Children ranged in age from infants to 25-year-old adults, with DACA-ineligible parents having older children. Table 2 shows that 56 of 61 children were US-born (73.8%) or DACA recipients (18%).

### Identified Themes

#### DACA Status Protects Against Deportation and Facilitates Access to Care

Intergroup comparison of DACA and DACA-ineligible parents shows the importance of DACA for family stability. DACA parents reported protection against deportation and increased access to medical services mainly through state health insurance assistance programs, particularly for those who lived in California as shown in Table 3. DACA-ineligible parents described their fear of family separation, anxiety about finding someone to take care of their children in case of deportation, and that they had had difficult conversations with their children about being deported. DACA-ineligible parents relied on emergency room visits and free clinics due to lack of insurance. They also reported traveling long distances to access free clinics, waiting for hours to see physicians, and feeling challenged by medical paperwork.

Adults with DACA, parents and nonparents, conveyed positive changes in their quality of life after receiving DACA. They also reported having better health care access compared to their DACA-ineligible family members. During their upbringing as children and young adults without DACA, they received medical care at varying levels of quality, depending on their residential state. Some considered moving across the United States to receive better care and avoid racist interactions with locals. Respondents reported predominantly positive experiences in Illinois and California because these states provide insurance to children regardless of their immigration status. This suggests that state-level pro or antiundocumented immigrant policies may contribute to security of health care access for participants: “It was through DACA. I was able to apply for Medicaid… it’s different now, I was able to get my wisdom teeth removed… she [mother] knows if I ever need anything, I’m covered. But then, for her, nothing has changed… She [sister] doesn’t go to the doctor much either. She’s undocumented and doesn’t have any way of getting insurance either. So, I’m the only one in my family right now that has health insurance.”(DACA respondent) “I don’t feel like I have stability. What if something changes, then it affects you. And I’m talking about legislation. If my mom gets deported tomorrow or whatever or if some program ends, I know that it affects me a lot.”(DACA respondent) “Right now, my son has Medicare with DACA and yes, he qualified…but my wife and I did not get that. We were left with just the one for emergency [Medicaid].”(DACA-ineligible respondent)

#### Parents Are Committed to Their Children’s Health Independent of Their DACA Status, But DACA-Ineligible Parents Neglect Their Own Health

Intergroup comparison of DACA and DACA-ineligible parents shows that they both ensured that their children visited a pediatrician regularly. DACA-ineligible parents in our sample deferred their own physical and mental health more than DACA parents. They did not view medical services for themselves as a necessity. They endured poor health before seeing a physician, and they disregarded medications for chronic illnesses because of the cost and the lack of permanent “solution” to their ailments. They also demonstrated a strong professed faith in traditional medical approaches to illness such as drinking tea. Yet, they were more action-oriented toward their children’s health: “My health is a bit deteriorated because of diabetes… I run out of the medications. Medical analysis is expensive. You realize you can’t afford your own disease… If my eldest son (US-born) has a fever, we run to the doctor. We can’t wait for the fever to drop… we also run if they break something or maybe a hit on the head….I would need a glucose meter and also test strips, but they also are expensive. Like 30 dollars. So, that’s another test I don’t do because I don’t want to spend money. They say, ‘Why don’t you? We’re talking about your health.’ Well, yes but am I just going to spend money in something doesn’t have a solution?”(DACA-ineligible parent)

#### Adults Who Received DACA as Children Exhibit Avoidance of Health Care

Interviews with individuals with DACA regarding their childhood experiences revealed that their behaviors as adults regarding health care mirrored those of their DACA-ineligible parents. DACA interviewees reported health behaviors similar to those of their DACA-ineligible parents. They would not see a physician and resorted to home remedies, despite having a legal status and health insurance. Moreover, some had memories of medical providers mistreating their parents because of language barriers. These experiences left them with weariness towards physicians, suggesting that DACA children of DACA-ineligible parents internalize their parents’ experiences with health care: “Researcher: You said insurance has made it easier to go to the doctor’s, and you’ve been able to get insurance— Medicaid, through DACA. What continues to deter you from going to the doctor?Interviewee: just how I’ve grown up. And feeling like, if it’s not severe, then I shouldn’t. It’s just what I’ve grown up with, and I feel like I’ve just kept that way of being. And I might still always keep it, even if I do have insurance to cover everything. I still try to back myself up from that now just because of how I grew up. My brother, he just got his DACA. And, for him, the only time he really goes to the doctor is for his heart checkup because of his heart malformation.”(DACA respondent) “When I’m about to die, that’s going to be considered an emergency… I probably would take myself to the emergency room rather than the doctor. With my kids, it’s a little bit different just because it’s my kids and I don’t want anything happening to them. So, if I know they need to go to the doctor like, I’ll take them to the doctor.”(DACA respondent)

#### Children of DACA-Ineligible Parents, Whether US-Born or DACA, Suffer From Psychosocial Stressor as a Result of Their Parents Health Situations

In addition to the concern about having their parents deported, children of DACA-ineligible parents, whether US-born or DACA, were stressed and burdened with helping their parents navigate a complex health care system. DACA-ineligible parents reported that their children accompanied them to free clinics because they had limited English proficiency and clinics often lacked translators. Even adults with DACA reported translating for their DACA-ineligible parents to communicate with physicians and complete medical paperwork. In the case of working-age children, whether US-born or with DACA, an authority role reversal sometimes occurred, so they served as the breadwinner of the house or paid for medical care when their parents were afflicted with chronic or severe illness.

These findings suggest that the well-being of children is linked to that of their DACA-ineligible parents even as the children get older and become adults. When DACA-ineligible parents were denied medical services, especially after work injuries, both parents and children suffered from the anxiety and depression this caused. The health of children of DACA-ineligible immigrants appeared to be impacted by the psychosocial stressors affecting their families: “At a young age, she [mother] had ovarian cancer … I had to step up. So, at junior year I took an under the table job at a casino…I worked graveyard shifts or swing shifts and I still went to high school. So, her being sick always made me feel like I was the mom. Then I didn’t have DACA until I was 18. But if I am sick, I can handle it…I avoid everything to do with the doctor. I really do not take care of myself the way I should.”(DACA respondent) “This [mother having schizophrenia] happened when she was 33 years old. We lived in Los Angeles, down-town and my mom was at the hospital all the time. We were living with our uncles for like a year. And after some time, they didn’t want to take care of us anymore. Daddy used to work and sometimes we were alone at home.”(DACA respondent) “Researcher: How did you react whenever your mom asked you to go to the doctor with you?Interviewee: I felt I needed to. I was there for translation purposes.”(DACA respondent)

## Discussion

Our study highlights that the DACA program lessens families’ anxiety about deportation and increases access to health care. Yet, many DACA recipients and US-born children live in families with mixed immigration status. They appear to experience heightened stress and worsening mental health when they witness their DACA-ineligible family members get deported or have limited to no access to medical services. For example, despite they themselves having medical insurance and protection from deportation, DACA recipients recounted the need to help their DACA-ineligible family members access medical services. Similarly, DACA and DACA-ineligible parents reported that their children, regardless of citizenship status, experienced the stress of helping their families obtain health care and navigate the health care system. Moreover, although DACA-ineligible parents prioritized their children’s health care, they deferred health care for themselves. Consequently, children witnessing their ineligible family members go without care causes stress in children. Furthermore, our findings suggest that mixed-status families’ interactions with the health care system may influence children’s health behaviors as future adults, as seen with DACA adults who reported avoiding preventive care and only utilizing health care when the need is extreme. This raises the question as to whether a similar behavior is being induced in US-born children in mixed-status families. Overall, if early negative family experiences with health care affects children’s future health behaviors, we need to consider this an intergenerational effect and address it accordingly in our health policies for immigrant families.

Overall, DACA has a positive effect on the lives of individuals who are undocumented. A number of qualitative studies indicate that the DACA program decreases the stress of possible deportation and creates more opportunities for economic stability.20,21 However, we should not underestimate the degree to which the politics of immigration leads to uncertainty of existence and chronic stress. Siemons et al reported increased stress among adolescents with DACA because of uncertainty of its continuance and greater family responsibilities for them.20 Our study expanded these findings by reporting for the first time on the stress of parents with and without DACA dealing with their children’s health. Our study also found that both children and adults with DACA experience the suffering of other undocumented family members from possible deportation and lack of health care, experiences that appear to influence their adult health behaviors.

Since the beginning of our nation, immigration policy has been influenced by politics, the flow of immigrants, and the need for immigrant labor.22 Today, national immigration policy has a varied impact on immigrants because of mixed responses from local and state jurisdictions. The Migration Policy Institute reports that between financial years 2016 and 2019, the US Immigration and Custom Enforcement doubled the number of detainment requests to local and state governments; however, there was a 300% decline in their execution by state and local jurisdictions.23 This decline occurred because of the “sanctuary” movement in states, counties, and cities. Currently, sanctuary states include California, Colorado, Connecticut, Illinois, Massachusetts, New Jersey, New Mexico, New York, Oregon, Vermont, and Washington.24 Yet, while immigrants in different parts of the United States are faced with diverse environments, a recent study suggests that documented immigrants who have been in the United States for less than 5 years are not relocating from states that have a 5-year stay requirement to gain access to government services to states that have eliminated this requirement.25 Whether this is also the case for undocumented immigrants seeking sanctuary states is unclear, since conditions in sanctuary states vary with regard to enforcement. For example, some of the states with the largest undocumented immigrant populations are not sanctuary states.26,27 Thus, studies on undocumented immigrants should take into account the state and local policies when interpreting and generalizing their results.

Nationally, health care access for undocumented immigrant is complex. It is currently estimated that approximately 11 million undocumented individuals live in the United States, with 5% being 16 years of age or less. Of those undocumented individuals who are 15 years or older, 42% are parents, 35% with and 7% without US-born children.28 At minimum, health care coverage for undocumented individuals includes emergency Medicaid. Although 66% of undocumented immigrants work, they have jobs that usually do not provide health insurance and consequently, are the highest proportion of uninsured, 45%.29 Although the development of the Affordable Care Act was to cover underserved populations, the legislation excluded undocumented immigrants, including those with DACA. Therefore, some states began examining ways to provide coverage to undocumented individuals, particularly children and pregnant women, through either expansion of their Medicaid programs or state-funded initiatives.29,30 Currently, 6 states and Washington DC cover undocumented children, including DACA (California, Illinois, Massachusetts, New York, Oregon, and Washington). California has also expanded coverage to young adults to age 25, and 16 states have expanded Children’s Health Insurance Program to cover unborn children as future citizens, thereby providing coverage for undocumented pregnant mothers. This is the status of our current patch-work of health care coverage for undocumented children and mothers. It demonstrates the need for a better national policy on health care coverage for immigrant families.

Limitations of this study include that it was based on a convenience sample drawn from a study on immigrants’ life transitions, primarily immigrants from Mexico living in California. This limited our analysis to themes on health collected for the original study and to conditions primarily affecting undocumented Mexican immigrants in California. Therefore, our findings may not be applicable to other DACA recipients from other countries or in other states. Nonetheless, this study, in a sanctuary state, identified themes on the intergenerational health effects of DACA on undocumented immigrants and their children, and highlighted future topics for research. Moreover, it demonstrated the usefulness of qualitative data on immigrant families to better understand the effects of policies that impact the adults and children in these families.

In conclusion, developing effective policy on immigration requires research that is mixed methods in order to understand its full impact on children and families. Our study presented qualitatively the positive impact of DACA on undocumented adults and their children, the next generation. Yet, it also highlighted the emotional burden felt by children as a result of the negative health experiences of their DACA-ineligible family members, suggesting the need to address health care of all family members. At a time when our nation is focusing on what to do about immigration, our nation of immigrants needs to recall our history of success when immigrants are given opportunities to have well-being and contribute to our nation.
